summary: Extends the Service Location Protocol so user agents can be told when a new service appears or one goes away, rather than only asking. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Instead of checking the bulletin board every few minutes, you can ask to be told when something new gets posted.

subtitle: Extends SLP so computers can be notified when services appear or disappear instead of polling.

tldr.problem: The Service Location Protocol (SLP) is demand-driven: clients must actively poll to find services. Applications that need timely notice of service changes must poll continuously, wasting network and processor resources.
tldr.mechanism: This protocol adds subscriptions to SLP. A client sends a subscription for a service type to a Directory Agent (DA) or multicast. Agents notify the subscriber by multicasting SLP registration and deregistration messages when that service type appears or disappears.
tldr.outcome: Clients receive event-driven notifications instead of polling. This reduces network traffic and improves responsiveness. The design scales from small networks (peer-to-peer multicast) to large networks (DA-coordinated multicast). The protocol is experimental and was not widely adopted.

today: RFC 3082 is an experimental extension to SLP for service notifications. While the design is sound, it did not see widespread deployment. Modern service discovery systems often use different approaches such as dynamic DNS, API-based service registries, or container orchestration platforms that handle service discovery and notification natively.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (RFC 2608) lets service agents advertise services and user agents discover them. It is demand-driven: a user agent must actively query to get service information. Some applications need timely notice when a service appears or disappears and cannot afford to poll repeatedly.

This RFC extends SLP with a subscription and notification mechanism. A user agent interested in a service type can subscribe, and service agents or directory agents will multicast a notification whenever a service of that type registers or deregisters. Notifications use existing SLP message types (SrvReg and SrvDereg) so implementation can reuse SLP code.

The design addresses two network sizes. In small networks without directory agents, service agents multicast notifications directly. In large networks, directory agents coordinate subscriptions and tell service agents which services to notify about. The scheme is distributed rather than centralized, so no single agent carries the load of all notifications.
sections.eli5: SLP normally requires computers to ask 'do you have a printer?' over and over. This extension lets computers register once to get told immediately when a printer appears or disappears.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The primary design goal is high scalability and robustness, matching the base SLP protocol. Notification must work in networks of any size without requiring directory agents in small networks. The load of notification delivery must be distributed so no single agent is overwhelmed.

Timeliness is important: user agents should receive notification promptly and regardless of which directory agent they connect to, since directory agents are transparent caches. Notifications should contain enough information about the triggering event that the user agent can decide relevance without issuing additional SLP requests in most cases.

The mechanism should be similar in small and large networks to reduce code complexity. Code reuse with base SLP is desirable; the mechanism uses existing SLP message types and the extension mechanism where possible. Finally, the system must remain robust when directory agents fail.
sections.eli5: The design wants to work in both tiny networks and huge enterprises, spread the work around so nothing gets overloaded, and reuse as much SLP code as possible.

sections.title: Small and Large Network Design
sections.content:
In small networks without directory agents, service agents broadcast or multicast their SrvReg (registration) and SrvDereg (deregistration) messages directly to user agents. The protocol uses multicast address 239.255.255.253 with port 1847 in IPv4, and scoped multicast addresses in IPv6. User agents join the multicast group to receive these notifications. Service agents notify whenever they come up or shut down, without checking for subscriptions.

In large networks with directory agents, a user agent attaches a Subscribe extension to its SrvRqst (service request). The directory agent responds with a SrvRply that includes a NotifyAt extension containing multicast group addresses. The user agent then listens on those groups. The directory agent informs existing service agents of the subscription by multicasting a DAAdvert (directory agent advertisement) with a NotifyAt extension. Service agents that match the subscription save the multicast addresses and notify on those groups when they register or deregister.

When a new service agent registers with a directory agent that has subscriptions, the directory agent includes a NotifyAt in the SrvAck (registration acknowledgement). The service agent then knows to multicast notifications. When a service advertisement times out, the directory agent itself multicasts a SrvDereg notification.
sections.eli5: Small networks: service agents just shout when they appear or disappear, and listeners hear. Large networks: the directory agent tells service agents where to shout and tells listeners where to listen.

sections.title: Subscribe and NotifyAt Extensions
sections.content:
The Subscribe extension is attached to a SrvRqst. It contains an abstract type flag that indicates whether the user agent wants concrete instances of an abstract service type or only a specific concrete type.

The NotifyAt extension contains a subscription lifetime, a list of scope names paired with multicast group addresses, and a service type name. The scope/group list tells agents where to multicast for each service type in each scope. An example IPv4 list is eng:239.255.255.42,corp:239.255.255.43, meaning the engineering scope uses group 239.255.255.42 and the corporate scope uses 239.255.255.43.

A user agent receives NotifyAt in the SrvRply response to its subscription. It then joins the multicast groups and listens on port 1847. A service agent receives NotifyAt in a multicast DAAdvert or in the SrvAck to its registration. The agent saves the groups and addresses, then multicasts its SrvReg (when it registers) or SrvDereg (when it shuts down) on those groups.
sections.eli5: The Subscribe extension asks for notifications. The NotifyAt extension tells you which multicast group addresses to listen to for each service type and scope.

sections.title: Multicast Address Allocation and Administration
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that enterprise networks deploy the Multicast Address Allocation Architecture (MAAA) with administratively scoped multicast and MADCAP (Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol). Each SLP scope should correspond to a multicast scope. When a user agent subscribes for a new service type in a scope, the directory agent allocates a unique multicast group address from that scope's range using MADCAP.

If MAAA is not deployed, the default SLP multicast address is used. The lifetime of each multicast group address allocation matches the subscription lifetime. When the subscription expires, the address allocation is released.

Network administrators must configure routers with administratively scoped multicast to limit the extent of multicast announcements. Without directory agents or MAAA in large networks, multicast traffic on the SLP multicast address could become very high, making DA deployment crucial in networks where notification is used.
sections.eli5: To avoid flooding the network with notifications, use MAAA and MADCAP to give each service type its own multicast group in the right scope. This way, only interested machines hear the notifications.
